target: Dyn ni wedi bod yn briod ers ugain mlynedd.
english: We've been married for twenty years.
tip: ‘ers’ marks how long something has held true: ‘ers ugain mlynedd’ = for twenty years. It normally pairs with the present tense.

target: Cafodd hi ei geni ym mil naw wyth pump.
english: She was born in nineteen eighty-five.
tip: ‘Was born’ is ‘cafodd’ plus a possessive plus ‘geni’, literally ‘got their birth’: ‘cafodd hi ei geni’ = she was born.

target: Mae ei llais hi'n cario ar draws yr ystafell.
english: Her voice carries across the room.
tip: Feminine ‘ei’ (her) is often echoed by ‘hi’ after the noun: ‘ei llais hi’ = her voice, which removes any his or her ambiguity.

target: Doedd hi ddim yn gallu cysgu oherwydd y sŵn.
english: She couldn't sleep because of the noise.
tip: Negative past of ‘bod’ uses ‘doedd’ with ‘ddim’: ‘doedd hi ddim’ = she was not.

target: Ymladodd ei thad-cu yn y rhyfel.
english: Her grandfather fought in the war.
tip: ‘ei’ meaning her aspirate-mutates p, t, c: ‘tad-cu’ becomes ‘thad-cu’, so ‘ei thad-cu’ = her grandfather.

target: Roedd deg cwestiwn ar y prawf.
english: There were ten questions on the test.
tip: ‘roedd’ is the was/were form of ‘bod’ for he, she or it: ‘roedd deg cwestiwn’ = there were ten questions.

target: Roedd ugain tŷ yn y pentref.
english: There were twenty houses in the village.
tip: Twenty has its own word, ‘ugain’, a leftover of the old base-twenty counting system: ‘ugain tŷ’ = twenty houses.

target: Bydda i'n ymarfer fy Nghymraeg bob nos.
english: I will practise my Welsh every evening.
tip: ‘bydda i’ is I will: ‘bydda i’n ymarfer’ = I will practise. Keep ‘yn’ before the verb, as in the present.

target: Roedd hi'n falch o lwyddiannau ei phlant.
english: She was proud of her children's achievements.
tip: ‘ei’ has two meanings: ‘ei’ (his) softens the next word, ‘ei’ (her) aspirates it. Here ‘ei phlant’ (her children) shows p to ph.

target: Bydd hi'n ysgrifennu llythyr at ei mam-gu.
english: She will write a letter to her grandmother.
tip: For writing or sending to a person, Welsh normally uses ‘at’, not ‘i’: ‘llythyr at ei mam-gu’ = a letter to her grandmother.

target: Mae ei deulu wedi byw yma ers cenedlaethau.
english: His family has lived here for generations.
tip: Masculine ‘ei’ (his) soft-mutates the next word: ‘teulu’ (family) becomes ‘ei deulu’ = his family.

target: Cafodd y gacen ei phobi gan fy mam-gu.
english: The cake was baked by my grandmother.
tip: Feminine ‘ei’ (her, its) aspirate-mutates p, t, c: ‘pobi’ becomes ‘phobi’ in ‘ei phobi’ = was baked.

target: Ddoe prynais i lyfr newydd yn y siop.
english: Yesterday I bought a new book at the shop.
tip: Starting with a time word like ‘ddoe’ doesn't change the verb: ‘prynais i’ still carries the ‘-ais’ ending for I bought.

target: Cefais i fy ngeni ar y pumed o Fawrth.
english: I was born on the fifth of March.
tip: ‘I was born’ is literally ‘I got my birth’: ‘cefais i fy ngeni’, using ‘cael’ plus ‘fy’ plus the verb.

target: Bydd hi'n dechrau ei swydd newydd ym mis Medi.
english: She will start her new job in September.
tip: ‘yn’ (in) becomes ‘ym’ before m: ‘ym mis Medi’ = in September.

target: Does dim amser gyda ni i gwblhau'r gwaith heddiw.
english: We have no time to complete the work today.
tip: Welsh has no verb ‘to have’. Use ‘gyda’ (with): ‘does dim amser gyda ni’ = we have no time, literally no time with us.

target: Dyw'r cawl ddim mor boeth ag oeddwn i'n disgwyl.
english: The soup is not as hot as I expected.
tip: ‘mor’ before an adjective, plus ‘â’ (or ‘ag’ before a vowel), means as...as: ‘mor boeth ag’ = as hot as.

target: Y ferch a enillodd y fedal aur yw fy nghyfnither.
english: The girl who won the gold medal is my cousin.
tip: ‘a’ marks a relative clause meaning who or which: ‘y ferch a enillodd y fedal’ = the girl who won the medal.

target: Pe bai'r trên ar amser, fyddwn i ddim yn hwyr.
english: If the train were on time, I wouldn't be late.
tip: ‘pe bai’ means if...were, for unreal or hypothetical situations: ‘pe bai'r trên ar amser’ = if the train were on time.

target: Aeth Trystan i brynu bara a chaws yn y farchnad.
english: Trystan went to buy bread and cheese at the market.
tip: ‘a’ (and) aspirate-mutates only the next word if it starts p, t or c: ‘caws’ becomes ‘chaws’, so ‘bara a chaws’ = bread and cheese.

target: Roedd e'n gweld eisiau ei deulu pan oedd e i ffwrdd.
english: He missed his family when he was away.
tip: ‘gweld eisiau’ means to miss someone, literally to see a want: ‘roedd e'n gweld eisiau’ = he missed.

target: Nid yn unig mae hi'n siarad Cymraeg, ond mae hi hefyd yn siarad Gwyddeleg.
english: Not only does she speak Welsh, but she also speaks Irish.
tip: ‘nid yn unig’ sets up not only, and pairs with ‘ond...hefyd’ (but also) later in the sentence.

target: Mae dau gi a dwy gath gyda ni.
english: We have two dogs and two cats.
tip: Two has separate genders: ‘dau gi’ = two dogs, but ‘dwy gath’ = two cats. Both soft-mutate the noun after them.

target: Rhaid i'r traethawd hir fod yn o leiaf deg mil o eiriau.
english: The dissertation must be at least ten thousand words.
tip: ‘rhaid i’ plus a subject means must: ‘rhaid i'r traethawd fod’ = the dissertation must be. Welsh frames obligation as necessity.

target: Gwnes i fy ngwaith cartref.
english: I did my homework.
tip: ‘fy’ (my) nasal-mutates the next word, turning g into ng: ‘gwaith’ becomes ‘ngwaith’ in ‘fy ngwaith’.

target: Does dim digon o gadeiriau.
english: There aren't enough chairs.
tip: ‘o’ (of) soft-mutates the noun after it: ‘cadeiriau’ becomes ‘gadeiriau’, so ‘digon o gadeiriau’ = enough chairs.

target: Hwyl fawr a phob bendith!
english: Goodbye and every blessing!
tip: ‘a’ (and) aspirate-mutates a following p, t or c: ‘pob’ becomes ‘phob’ here in ‘a phob bendith’.

target: Does dim amser i'w wastraffu.
english: There's no time to waste.
tip: ‘i'w’ is ‘i’ plus ‘ei’ (to its) and soft-mutates the verb: ‘gwastraffu’ becomes ‘wastraffu’ in ‘i'w wastraffu’ = to waste it.

target: Arhoswch funud os gwelwch yn dda.
english: Wait a minute please.
tip: The ‘-wch’ ending marks a plural or polite command: ‘arhoswch’ = wait, said to more than one person or formally.

target: Daeth ei rhieni o Ynys Môn.
english: Her parents came from Anglesey.
tip: ‘dod’ (to come) is irregular in the past: ‘daeth’ = came, not a regular ending. ‘daeth ei rhieni’ = her parents came.
